Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Kiet Phạm is a 41-year-old Vietnamese American dancer and choreographer who has spent the better part of two decades building a career that centers on discipline, precision, and the communication of human experience through physical form. He is married, softly spoken in sessions, and arrived at the intake appointment wearing rehearsal clothes, as though he had come directly from the studio — which, his wife later confirmed, he almost never does anymore.

Three years ago, Kiet volunteered for a six-month deployment with an international humanitarian organization operating in a conflict zone in the Middle East. He had done shorter stints before and described that earlier work as among the most meaningful of his life. The deployment that broke him began ordinarily enough: distributing medical supplies, coordinating shelter logistics, working alongside local staff he had come to genuinely trust. Then, on a late afternoon in early spring — the light low and golden, the air carrying the particular smell of a generator running too hot — a coordinated attack struck the compound. In the chaos that followed, Kiet made a decision. A colleague, a young local interpreter named Tariq, was injured and calling out. Kiet reached him and began to move him, but when secondary explosions started and armed men entered the compound, Kiet ran. He left Tariq where he lay. Tariq did not survive. The smell of burning fuel and scorched concrete was everywhere as Kiet pressed himself into a drainage channel and waited, and the men who passed above him smelled heavily of alcohol.

Kiet returned to the United States four months later, outwardly functional but privately dismantling. In the weeks that followed, he found that late afternoon — that particular quality of fading light around four or five o'clock — would arrive each day carrying something he could not name at first. He would be in the studio, moving through a warm-up, and the angle of the sun through the high windows would shift, and suddenly he was not in the studio at all. The memory did not arrive as recollection. It arrived as the thing itself: the sound, the heat, the smell of burning, Tariq's voice. Kiet described it in session as being pulled through a hole in the floor. There was no transition, no warning. One moment he was marking choreography, the next he was back in that drainage channel, certain the danger was still present and immediate.

The smell of alcohol — at a dinner party, at a colleague's post-show celebration — produced the same collapse of time and place. So did the smell of anything burnt: a candle extinguished too quickly, a pan left on the stove. His wife learned to open windows before lighting incense. Kiet learned to leave rooms without explaining why.

What Kiet found hardest to speak about was not the intrusions themselves but what accompanied the memory when it surfaced: a flooding, annihilating shame. He had come to believe, with a certainty that resisted any gentle challenge, that what he did in that compound revealed something true and permanent about his character — that he was not the person he had understood himself to be. He felt he had acted in a way that violated everything he valued: loyalty, courage, the willingness to remain present for another person's suffering. He also believed that his responses since — the avoidance, the sleeplessness, the way he had slowly withdrawn from the very practice that once anchored him — confirmed that he was failing at recovery in a way that other people simply would not. He was certain he could not trust his own judgment or his own steadiness, and this certainty had consequences. He had turned down two significant choreographic commissions. He had stopped teaching the evening classes that once filled his schedule, because four o'clock would come and the studio light would change and he could not be responsible for a room full of students while that was happening to him.

It was his wife who finally made the appointment, after a dinner at which Kiet left the table without a word when a guest opened a bottle of wine. He came to the first session hoping, more than anything, to be told that what he did was not what he believed it was. He was afraid, he said quietly, that therapy would confirm it was.
